phenotypic heterogeneity can affect the evolution of cancer.
the evolutionary advantage of malignant mutants in a heterogeneous population of SCs depends not only on their growth rate, but also on the rates of their differentiation and dedifferentation.

the evolution of cancer in the context of a heterogeneous population structure.

the evolution of malignancy in heterogeneous populations of stem cells and their associated progenitor is more complex and less straightforward than in a homogeneous population of SCs.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have derived a novel mathematical model for selection in a complex heterogeneous system, with applications in biology, ecology, and population genetics.

the evolutionary advantage of a mutation depends on the population structure, the mutation rate, the growth rates, the mutation-induced fitness, the mutation-induced plasticity, and the polarity between stem and progenitor cell turnover.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of cancer is a highly complex process, and that it cannot be understood without considering the population dynamics of both stem and non-stems cells, as well as their interactions.
a complex phenotypic heterogeneity of a population can have a significant effect on evolutionary dynamics.
a population of heterogeneous sub-populations is a very powerful evolutionary mechanism, which can be exploited by the evolution of malignancy in cancer progression.
